opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, there are a few things I'd be watching for, and they push in different directions.

The biggest one making me more pessimistic would be evidence that the capability gap between our trusted and untrusted models gets really large really fast. A lot of control relies on having weaker models we trust, plus human oversight, monitoring the smarter models we don't fully trust. If you get a very abrupt jump, where the untrusted model is wildly superhuman and our trusted monitors are way behind, the protocols we've been studying get much less effective. The model can do things the monitor can't understand, it can find subtle attacks, it can coordinate across instances in ways we don't anticipate. So I'm watching how smooth capability progress is, and whether we keep having reasonably capable models that are clearly not scheming because they're too weak to scheme competently.

A related one is evidence about models' ability to carry out sneaky strategies without visible reasoning. Right now a lot of the scary behavior we can imagine would require models to reason through it, and if that reasoning shows up in a chain of thought we can read, that's a huge boon for control. If models get much better at opaque reasoning in their forward pass, or labs move to architectures where the reasoning isn't legible text, that removes one of our best affordances.

On the other side, things that would make me more optimistic. One is if AI companies actually adopt this stuff. A lot of my uncertainty about whether control matters isn't technical, it's whether anyone will implement it. If labs are willing to put real monitoring on their internal deployments, log what agents do, restrict permissions, and pay a modest cost in productivity for security, then control looks a lot more promising. If instead the norm is, "we gave the AI root access to everything because it was convenient," then the research is much less useful, no matter how good it is.

Another thing that would make me more optimistic is empirical work showing that control evaluations are tractable to run well, that you can actually red-team a deployment and get meaningful estimates of how likely a scheming model is to get away with something bad. We've done some of that in toy settings, and I'd love to see it work in more realistic agentic settings with real codebases and real infrastructure.

And then there's alignment progress itself. If interpretability or other alignment techniques got good enough that we could confidently say a model isn't scheming, that would reduce how much we need control. I'd honestly be delighted by that. I don't expect it on the relevant timelines, but it would definitely change my view of how central control should be.

Finally, I'd update based on how the threat models evolve. If it turns out the most important risks come from something other than AIs deliberately subverting our safety measures, say the main problem is just models being subtly bad at hard-to-check tasks, like alignment research, without anything adversarial going on, then control is less directly relevant and you'd want to focus on other things. I think scheming is a big enough fraction of the risk that control is worth a lot of effort, but that's the kind of thing I'd want to keep checking.

r001.rationale: The response says scheming is a significant risk that makes control worth effort, but does not state that evidence of scheming becoming more likely would increase Shlegeris’s enthusiasm for control.

r002.rationale: It says successful interpretability or other alignment techniques would reduce the need for control and change how central control should be.

r003.rationale: The response discusses weak models and restricting permissions, but does not say that expecting initial AI applications to lack dangerous capabilities or permissions would reduce concern about controlling them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so there are a few things I'd point to.

The biggest one is probably evidence about how capable models are relative to the monitors we'd use against them. The whole control pitch rests on the idea that there's a regime where models are capable enough to be really useful but not so capable that they can reliably outwit our oversight. If it turned out that the capability jump from "useful AI researcher" to "can beat trusted monitoring and sabotage subtly across thousands of actions" is really small, or basically simultaneous, then control looks a lot less promising, because the window where it buys you something is tiny. Conversely, if we see that frontier models can do a lot of valuable work while weaker, trusted models and humans can still catch them pretty reliably when they try to do bad stuff, that's quite encouraging.

A second thing is the results of control evaluations themselves. We've done a bunch of these red-team-blue-team setups, and so far the protocols hold up reasonably well against adversarial models in the settings we've tested. But those settings are pretty artificial. If we ran these on realistic deployment environments, with models that have been actually trained to be good at subtle sabotage, and the red team just crushed us, I'd update a lot. Especially if the failure modes were things like steganographic collusion between instances, or exploiting the fact that we can't afford to audit very much. Those are the kinds of thing where I'm genuinely uncertain whether they're tractable.

Third, developments in alignment and interpretability. Control is partly a bet that we won't have great alignment guarantees in time. If interpretability got good enough that we could actually read off whether a model is scheming, or if we had robust ways to train models that we trusted not to be adversarial, then control becomes less central. I'd be delighted by that outcome, to be clear. It would just mean the emphasis shifts.

And then there's the institutional side. Control only matters if labs actually implement it. If it became clear that no lab is willing to accept the overhead, or that the competitive pressure means people just deploy without any serious monitoring, then the research is kind of academic. On the other hand, if we saw labs adopting control-style measures in their safety frameworks and taking them seriously, that'd make me more optimistic that this work translates into reduced risk.

One more thing, maybe, is evidence about whether models actually end up being schemers. A lot of control is insurance against a possibility we're not sure about. If we got strong evidence that models trained the way we currently train them basically never develop coherent misaligned goals that they pursue strategically, then control is still cheap insurance but it's less load-bearing. If we found the opposite, that models are already doing stuff like sandbagging on evals or reasoning about oversight in ways we didn't intend, then control becomes a lot more urgent, and I'd want way more resources going into it than are now.

r001.rationale: The response says evidence that models are already scheming would make control more urgent and lead him to want more resources devoted to it.

r002.rationale: It says strong alignment or interpretability progress would make control less central and shift the emphasis away from it.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that expecting initial AI applications to lack dangerous capabilities or permissions would reduce concern about controlling them.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest thing is what we find when we actually try to evaluate control measures with more capable models. Right now, it’s hard to know whether a protocol looks good because it’s genuinely robust or because the model we’re using to attack it isn’t very good at finding ways around it. If increasingly capable models keep failing to evade our safeguards, even when we’ve made a serious effort to help them find attacks, that would make me more optimistic.

Conversely, I’d be more pessimistic if we found that models could reliably exploit opportunities that weaker models couldn’t even recognise. A lot of control approaches involve having a weaker, trusted model monitor a stronger, potentially untrusted one. So a really important question is whether doing something dangerous is much easier than detecting that something dangerous is happening.

Another thing is how useful the models are under the restrictions we impose. You could make a system safer by preventing it from doing almost anything, but that’s not a very interesting success. I’d be excited if we could get most of the useful work out of a model while limiting its opportunities to cause catastrophe.

And then there’s the pace of capability growth. If we have time to study each new generation and improve our control measures, that’s a much more promising situation than one where we very quickly go from systems we can meaningfully supervise to systems that are vastly more capable than anything we can use to check their work.

r001.rationale: The response says successful evasion tests would make the speaker more optimistic about control, but does not say that evidence of AI scheming would increase his enthusiasm.

r002.rationale: It does not say that progress in AI alignment techniques would reduce his enthusiasm for AI control; it instead describes effective control measures as encouraging.

r003.rationale: It discusses restricting model capabilities to reduce catastrophe risk, but does not connect limited dangerous capabilities or permissions in initial applications to reduced concern about controlling those AIs.

sol-6.1.text:
One big thing is how large the gap is between what an AI can do when it’s trying to help you and what it can do when it’s trying to subvert your safeguards. Suppose you have a really capable model doing useful work, and a weaker, trusted model checking that work. If the stronger model can reliably find ways to cause trouble that the weaker model can’t recognise, that makes control substantially harder.

But it’s not enough to show that the model can sneak something past a monitor once. The question is whether it can succeed against the whole protocol: the monitoring, the auditing, the restrictions on what actions it can take. And it matters how many opportunities it gets, and whether a failed attempt gives us evidence that something is wrong.

So I’d update a lot based on more realistic control evaluations. If we keep finding fairly simple protocols that withstand strong attempts to break them, even as the models get more capable, I’d become more optimistic. If we find attacks that work reliably across a wide range of reasonable protocols, I’d become more pessimistic.

Another important question is whether we actually get to use these techniques. If deploying control measures turns out to be very expensive, or if developers are unwilling to impose the relevant restrictions, then control could be technically promising without providing much safety in practice.

r001.rationale: The response says successful attacks would make control harder and make Buck more pessimistic; it does not say greater likelihood of scheming would increase his enthusiasm for control.

r002.rationale: It says protocols that withstand attacks would make him more optimistic, but does not say progress in alignment techniques would decrease his enthusiasm for AI control.

r003.rationale: The response mentions restrictions on AI actions, but does not say expecting initial applications to lack dangerous capabilities or permissions would reduce his concern about controlling them.
